1.0.s.en: 1. The Lord goes out to judgment:

1.0.0.en: 1 The word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. 2 Hear, all ye people; hearken, O earth, and all that therein is: and let the Lord GOD be witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple. 3 For, behold, the LORD cometh forth out of his place, and will come down, and tread upon the high places of the earth. 4 And the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire, and as the waters that are poured down a steep place.

1.0.1.en: The word of the LORD that came to Micah the Morasthite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. [1]

1.0.2.en: "The word of the Lord," or "the word of Yahweh": the prophet affirms that what he utters and what he writes is not from himself, but is the message of Yahweh, carrying divine authority. Yahweh directed this message to His prophet Micah so that he might proclaim it to the people as well as to the leaders.

1.0.3.en: The name of the prophet, like that of other prophets such as Hosea, Joel and Obadiah, reveals his message. The word "Micah," as we have seen, means "none is like Yahweh," although St. Ambrose sees that its meaning is "one with God." It is as though the prophet is challenging the false prophets and the stubborn, wicked and resisting ones, that there is none like Yahweh, and that He cannot be resisted!

1.0.4.en: St. Jerome sees that the word "Moresheth" in Hebrew means "my possessions," and for this reason he sees in Micah one who possesses Christ or who is an heir with Him. If the Book of Micah began with the public trial brought by God Himself, then in His case, even when He chastens, He does not take vengeance, but desires to qualify us for the eternal inheritance and heavenly glory.

1.0.5.en: * "Micah: its meaning is "one with God," or, as we find in another place, "one is the son of the Morasthite," that is, "the son of the heir." Who is the Heir but the Son of God, who says: "All things are delivered unto me of my Father" (Mt 11:27)? He who is the Heir desires us to be partakers in the inheritance.

1.0.6.en: You ask well: Who is Micah? He is not of the people, but he was chosen to receive the grace of God, and the Holy Spirit speaks through him. He began his prophecy in the days of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. But this order in the presentation of the vision to him has its meaning, for it begins with the age of wicked kings and ends with a good king.

1.0.7.en: St. Ambrose As for his saying "which he saw," it does not mean a bodily sight, but a spiritual vision by the mind, for the Spirit of the Lord opened the eyes of Micah to perceive the message which he is bound to witness to and proclaim to the people.

1.0.8.en: Micah prophesied in the age of Ahaz, who is considered one of the worst kings of Judah, and he also prophesied in the age of Hezekiah, the godly man of reform. In the age of Ahaz he did not fear to speak of God's chastenings of Judah, but he opened the door of consolations for the holy souls returning to the Lord. And in the reign of the godly Hezekiah he spoke of the necessity of inner spiritual reform. Thus, with the changing circumstances of the times, the word of God remains firm: it does not flatter the wicked, nor does it close the door of hope before them, nor does it delight in outward reforms without entering into the depths.

1.0.10.en: Hearken, O earth, and all that therein is.

1.1.0.en: And let the Lord GOD be witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple. [2]

1.1.1.en: Since many of the people of God stopped their ears from listening to the voice of the Lord, He extended the call to the earth that it might open its ears and listen to Him. As the Lord Christ said: "That many shall come from the east and west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven" (Mt 8:11).

1.1.2.en: God, who loves His heavenly and earthly creation, often summons them to listen to His word (Isa 1:2; Deut 32:1); He asks them to listen to Him with attentive ears, even when He judges His people, for He desires to reveal to all the secrets of His dealings with His creation. There is no partiality with God: if His people sin, He calls the Gentiles to attend their trial, that it may be a practical lesson for their acceptance of the faith.

1.1.3.en: He is the Lord of all creation and its Master; He speaks from His holy temple, that is, from heaven, which is consecrated to Him as the Holy One. From there He speaks, longing that all creation be sanctified and become a living icon of the Holy One. Whether He chastens or shows tenderness, the aim of the Holy One is the holiness of His creation.

1.1.4.en: * "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification" (1 Thess 4:3)... Notice how he does not look to any subject with such zeal as this. For he writes of it in another place: "Follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord" (Heb 12:14). Why should we marvel if he writes to his disciples about this matter everywhere? In his epistle to Timothy he says: "keep thyself pure" (1 Tim 5:22), and in his second epistle to the Corinthians he says: "In much patience, in fastings, in pureness" (2 Cor 6:5-6).

1.1.5.en: St. John Chrysostom Since the rational people became corrupt and acted irrationally against their Creator, the Creator wished to rebuke them through irrational nature; so He often summoned the lifeless earth and the heaven with its stars, by the mouth of the prophets, to witness His judgment of His people. So it is no wonder that the earth moved and quaked when the hand of the creature was stretched out to crucify the incarnate divine Word, and that the sun withheld its rays to reprove the ungrateful crucifiers and bear witness against them with darkness.

1.1.6.en: The creation which God brought into being to serve man became a witness against him and a reprover of him for his disobedience and corruption.

1.2.0.en: For, behold, the LORD cometh forth out of his place, and will come down, and tread upon the high places of the earth. [3]

1.2.1.en: God used to go out to His people so that He might bring them out to Himself, and to come down to them in His love so as to lift them up into His embrace. Now, since they persisted in corruption in stubbornness, He went out to judge them and chasten them.

1.2.2.en: The prophet portrays God as coming down from heaven, walking upon the mountains, to shatter Samaria for its insistence on the worship of idols and its practice of abominations; and its corruption had crept into Judah, so that the judgment of Judah too was at the doors.

1.2.3.en: The Lord's coming down and treading upon the high places of the earth points to two things. First, that the Word of God, the Creator and Savior, goes forth as though from His place, for He says of His incarnation and becoming man: "for I proceeded forth and came from God" (Jn 8:42); and second, that the Lord sits upon the throne of His mercy, and when He chastens firmly He appears as one who goes out of His place to shatter the pride and loftiness of man. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: "For, behold, the LORD cometh out of his place to punish" (Isa 26:21). He is a heavenly Father who longs not to punish; if He chastens, it is as one who has gone out of His place, that is, out of mercy full of tenderness and compassion. Our iniquity and disobedience make Him as one who goes out of His place to punish... Even in His going out He seeks to gather us to Himself, to bring us back to the throne of His mercy.

1.2.4.en: Some see that He is pointing here to the Lord's going out as upon the clouds to judge the wicked who exalt themselves, and to glorify His humble believers.

1.2.5.en: * Let us now consider the statement of Jesus: "for I proceeded forth and came from God" (Jn 8:42). It seems useful to me to set beside these words the following words from Micah: "Hear, O my people, my words, and let the earth and all that therein is hearken, and let the Lord be a witness in the midst of you, the Lord from the holy house. For, behold, the LORD cometh forth out of his place, and treadeth upon the high places of the earth, and the mountains shall be moved under him, and the valleys shall melt as wax before the fire, and as the waters that are poured down a steep place" (Mic 1:2-4). Now consider whether the statement "I proceeded forth from God" is equivalent to this statement; since the Son is in the Father, being in the form of the Father before He emptied Himself (Phil 2:6-7), He was God in His place, so it appears as though contradictory that He goes forth from the Father and at the same time is still in God.

1.2.6.en: * It is said that God comes down when He condescends to give attention to human weakness. This must be discerned especially in the case of our Lord and Savior, who, since He "thought it not robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, and took upon him the form of a servant" (Phil 2:6-7), in this way came down. For "no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven" (Jn 3:13). For the Lord came down, not only to care for us but also to bear what is ours, since He "took upon him the form of a servant"; and though He Himself is invisible by nature, being equal with the Father, yet He took a visible form, since He "was found in fashion as a man" (Phil 2:7).

1.2.7.en: Origen And the mountains shall be molten under him, and the valleys shall be cleft, as wax before the fire.

1.3.0.en: And as the waters that are poured down a steep place. [4]

1.3.1.en: When the Lord goes out to judge His people, the mountains and the high places used for the worship of idols cannot stand before Him, those which represent impregnable fortresses to protect them from any foreign invasion; for the Lord treads upon them, and they melt and become dust. Nor can the valleys support them, for they melt before Him like wax before the fire. Neither the great men, who reckon themselves lofty mountains, nor those of the lower classes, who are like the valleys, can defend the wicked people before God.

1.3.2.en: It is related in the Coptic (Bohairic) Life of St. Pachomius: [On another occasion, as (his disciple Theodore) was sitting by himself in a place reading the book of the Twelve Prophets, he came to the prophet Micah. An angel of the Lord appeared to him and asked him about this verse from Micah: "as the waters that are poured down a steep place." He said to him: "What do you think is the meaning of this?" And as he was perplexed about it, trying to understand, the angel answered him: "Theodore, why have you not grasped its meaning? Is it not clear that it is the water of the river that flows down from Paradise?" And when the angel had said this, he no longer saw him].

1.3.3.en: * Like wax, which cannot bear to approach the fire, and like water flowing down, so will all the wicked be when the Lord comes, for they dissolve and vanish.

1.4.0.en: 5 For the transgression of Jacob is all this, and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the transgression of Jacob? is it not Samaria? and what are the high places of Judah? are they not Jerusalem? 6 "Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof. 7 And all the graven images thereof shall be beaten to pieces, and all the hires thereof shall be burned with the fire, and all the idols thereof will I lay desolate: for she gathered it of the hire of an harlot, and they shall return to the hire of an harlot."

1.4.1.en: For the transgression of Jacob is all this, and for the sins of the house of Israel.

1.4.2.en: What is the transgression of Jacob? is it not Samaria?

1.4.3.en: And what are the high places of Judah? are they not Jerusalem? [5]

1.4.4.en: He began with Samaria, the capital of Israel, as the center of the worship of Baal, from which idolatrous worship seeped into Judah. Then he spoke of the high places of Judah, where idolatrous worship crept in. Samaria was punished first at the hand of Assyria, and afterward Jerusalem, the capital of Judah, at the hand of Babylon.

1.4.5.en: By the high places here he points to the worship of idols that was carried on there, which the Law forbade (Deut 13).

1.4.6.en: Sadly, the focus of sin in the two kingdoms was the two capitals: Samaria and Jerusalem.

1.5.0.en: Therefore I will make Samaria as an heap of the field, and as plantings of a vineyard: and I will pour down the stones thereof into the valley, and I will discover the foundations thereof. [6]

1.5.1.en: Here he presents a terrifying judgment as the natural fruit of the iniquity of Samaria. Samaria was turned into a ruin because of continual wars (Isa 21:1-3). God allows Samaria to be shattered and its stones to be poured down into the valley, so that its foundations are completely laid bare. To this day Samaria is heaps of stones, not only on the hill, but even in the fields below, and archaeologists have uncovered the foundations of the palaces of Omri and Ahab.

1.5.2.en: Samaria, which prided itself on its wealth and the multitude of its inhabitants, becomes heaps of refuse of vineyards and fields and of stones. They were gathered together to be cast out. Perhaps he began with the plantings of vineyards and afterward the heaps of stones, because Samaria was originally vineyard fields before it was built up as a capital, as though it returns to what it was, and even to something worse, for the buildings collapse and are turned into heaps of stones, losing their nature as a royal capital to become a ruin.

1.6.0.en: And all the graven images thereof shall be beaten to pieces, and all the hires thereof shall be burned with the fire, and all the idols thereof will I lay desolate: for she gathered it of the hire of an harlot, and they shall return to the hire of an harlot. [7]

1.6.1.en: The prophet looked at the civilization that Samaria had attained, which came only through idol worship, as well as from the hire of harlots; so it is fitting that its graven images be beaten to pieces, because they were made from the hire of harlots.

1.6.2.en: Many harlots used to offer from the hire of harlotry to the pagan temples, to be spent on them and for their adornment; so when these temples collapse with their abominations, it is as though they returned what they had received to the harlots.

1.7.0.en: 8 Therefore I will wail and howl, I will go stripped and naked: I will make a wailing like the dragons, and mourning as the owls. 9 For her wound is incurable; for it is come unto Judah; he is come unto the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem.

1.7.1.en: Danger threatens Jerusalem, for the Assyrian army sweeps over the coastal plain in the direction of Egypt, bursting into the place where Micah dwelt, crossing from one city to another, and reaching the walls of Jerusalem. The prophet Isaiah described the same situation while dwelling inside the city (Isa 10:28-34), whereas Micah described it from outside the city, at a distance of about 20 miles.

1.7.2.en: Therefore I will wail and howl.

1.7.3.en: I will go stripped and naked.

1.7.4.en: I will make a wailing like the dragons. [8]

1.7.5.en: As the prophet laments for Israel, he does not cease weeping and crying out until his voice becomes like the voice of the jackals, and like the voice of the young of the female ostrich.

1.7.6.en: Captives used to be led barefoot and naked; so the soul of the prophet was embittered, and he became like a captive of grief, losing his garments and his sandals, to walk in the road barefoot and naked.

1.7.7.en: Earlier, the prophet Isaiah had walked barefoot and naked for three years at the command of the Lord, as a sign and wonder upon Egypt and Ethiopia (Cush), a prophecy of their captivity at the hand of Assyria (Isa 20:2-4).

1.7.8.en: * Isaiah's walking naked without shame was a symbol of the coming captivity. Jeremiah was sent from Jerusalem to the Euphrates, and left his girdle to rot in the camp of the Chaldeans among the Assyrians, the enemies of his people (Jer 13:6-7)... He urges men to repent.

1.7.9.en: St. Jerome * The captivity of our brothers must be reckoned as though it were our own captivity. The sorrows of those in danger are our sorrows. You must be sure that there is one body of our unity. It is not our love alone but also our religion that moves and encourages us to rescue the members of our family.

1.7.10.en: St. Cyprian Whoever looks at the prophet Micah, weeping and lamenting, walking stripped of his outer garment, barefoot, makes light of him as a naked and barefoot peasant. But heaven looks at him and sees in his tears, his cries, his nakedness and his bare feet the image of wonderful love, which sees its people about 150 years later in captivity, and so reckons itself a captive with them and shares with them the bitterness of their souls. As St. Paul says: "Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; and them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body" (Heb 13:3). And his saying: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor 11:29).

1.7.11.en: For her wound is incurable, and mourning as the owls.

1.8.0.en: For it is come unto Judah; he is come unto the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem. [9]

1.8.1.en: The corruption of Samaria and its worship of idols spread in Israel, and crept into Judah, until it reached the gates of Jerusalem, and she shared with it its evil.

1.8.2.en: The wounds became incurable, on the spiritual, social and political levels; this is what befell Jerusalem.

1.8.3.en: The "gate of the city" in the East referred to the men of state who worked with the king and to his counselors; they used to gather at the gate of the city. This continued even in the days of the Turks, for the Turkish Sultan with his entourage was called "the Sublime Porte." Sublime Porte.

1.9.0.en: 10 Declare ye it not at Gath, weep ye not at all: in the house of Aphrah roll thyself in the dust. 11 Pass ye away, thou inhabitant of Saphir, having thy shame naked: the inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth in the mourning of Beth-ezel; he shall receive of you his standing. 12 For the inhabitant of Maroth waited carefully for good: but evil came down from the LORD unto the gate of Jerusalem. 13 O thou inhabitant of Lachish, bind the chariot to the swift beast: she is the beginning of the sin to the daughter of Zion: for the transgressions of Israel were found in thee. 14 Therefore shalt thou give presents to Moresheth-gath: the houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel. 15 Yet will I bring an heir unto thee, O inhabitant of Mareshah: he shall come unto Adullam the glory of Israel. 16 Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children; enlarge thy baldness as the eagle; for they are gone into captivity from thee.

1.9.1.en: The prophet Micah points to ten cities, the first five north of Jerusalem, and the last southwest of Jerusalem or south of it. It is as though destruction will come not upon Jerusalem alone, but upon the cities surrounding it also. All these cities are pagan. Destruction will come upon all, so long as they insist on their evil.

1.9.2.en: Some scholars see that some of them bear symbolic names, which reveal the role of sin and its hideousness in the life of the community, as in the life of the person determined on his evil. 1. A stumbling block: the prophet asks the inhabitants of Jerusalem, when captivity comes upon them after a century and a half, not to tell the pagan cities of Philistia, such as Gath and Acco (Acre), what has befallen them [10], and not to weep before their inhabitants, for they have become a stumbling block to them. Moreover, the word "Acco" is derived from the Hebrew word that means weeping. 2. Return to dust: instead of the heaven prepared for the believer, the person determined on his evil wallows in the dust, and hears the divine voice: "Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return," and so he becomes Aphrah (dust) [10].

1.9.3.en: * There is nothing that weighs down the soul and presses upon it and brings it down below like the sense of sin, and there is nothing that gives it wings and lifts it to the heights like the attainment of righteousness and virtue.

1.10.0.en: St. John Chrysostom 3. The stripping of the garment of righteousness: if the word "Shaphir" means beauty, then sin strips man of the garment of righteousness, and Shaphir becomes naked and ashamed [11] instead of the inner beauty of the soul. 4. A sudden distress: the word "Zaanan" means "city of the flock." As the people are surprised, like a flock of sheep, by the calamity that comes upon them as the fruit of their sins, from the horror of the surprise they do not go out of the city, but all walk around one another, and everyone stumbles. Perhaps this happens because the calamity falls upon the whole community. 5. A general calamity: the word "Beth-ezel" means "a nearby place." So everyone stands in his place, and there is none who goes out to his near neighbor to seek his help, since the calamity falls upon all. 6. Bitterness of soul: the word "Maroth" means "bitter." The wicked person may think that he enjoys good things and pleasures by practicing evil and sin, but soon he loses his good things and his life is turned into an unbearable bitterness. 7. The demolition of fortresses and the loss of security: Lachish was one of the most fortified cities of Judah, thinking that the enemy would not be able to storm it. But the prophet Micah sees with the eye of prophecy Sennacherib besieging it, and sees its storming (Isa 36:1-2). Its men try to flee with their chariots and horses, but to where? They were driven into captivity.

1.10.1.en: * As those who come out of earthly prisons are brought bound in their chains to the place of trial, so all souls bound with the chains of their various sins are led to the dreadful judgment seat.

1.10.2.en: * When you see the rich man entangled in his countless affairs, do not reckon him rich, but in this he is wretched. For he is in these chains under the authority of a harsh jailer: the evil love of riches. Because of this he is not permitted to depart from the prison, but is bound with thousands of chains and guards and doors and bolts (locks), and when he is cast into the inner prison it tracks him down so that he may feel pleasure in these chains, so that he finds no hope of deliverance from the evils that press upon him.

1.10.3.en: St. John Chrysostom 8. There is no salvation by mere human wisdom: even the prophet's own city, Moresheth-gath, gives gifts to flatter the Philistines into helping it, but to no avail. 9. Lies and deception: the word "Achzib" means "a lie" or "deception," for the people were deceived by the false prophets, and thought that they were in peace and security, but we shall uncover their deception after it is too late. She becomes an inheritance for the enemy; Achzib is joined with Mareshah, but discovers her inability to help, since Mareshah herself becomes an inheritance for the enemy. 10. The loss of glory: the great and the nobles flee to Adullam, famous for its caves. They try to hide in the caves, and so the glory of Judah becomes imprisoned in them. 11. Unceasing mourning: it was among the ancient customs to cut the hair, especially for girls and women, at the death of someone dear to them, and when they are carried away into captivity. So baldness here points to the lack of consolation, like one who has lost his dearest or been led away as a captive.

1.10.4.en: Declare ye it not at Gath, weep ye not at all.

1.10.5.en: In the house of Aphrah roll thyself in the dust. [10]

1.10.6.en: Rolling in the dust points to intense grief.

1.10.7.en: Aphrah is a Hebrew name meaning "dust." Beth Aphrah lies on the slope of the mountains of Judah, and its location is not known precisely; J. Simons sees that it is the Wadi el-Afr between ed-Dawaimeh and Tell ed-Duweir. Some see that it is et-Taiyibeh between Hebron and Beit Jibrin.

1.10.8.en: Pass ye away, thou inhabitant of Saphir, having thy shame naked.

1.10.9.en: The inhabitant of Zaanan came not forth.

1.10.10.en: In the mourning of Beth-ezel; he shall receive of you his standing. [11]

1.10.11.en: Shaphir: Shaphir, Saphir, a Hebrew name meaning "beautiful," a city in Judah; some see that it is now Tell es-Suwafir, which lies three and a half miles southeast of Ashdod, and others consider it more likely to be "Khirbet el-Kom" (Kherbet el-Kom) west of Hebron, which lies in the "Wadi es-Saffar," in which the echo of the ancient name is heard.

1.10.12.en: He likens these cities to a woman who loses every possibility of covering herself, and so walks among men naked and ashamed. She is led as a captive in great disgrace, and no man can move to rescue her from the violent enemy.

1.10.13.en: * Would that we rid ourselves of the filth of sin, so that the original beauty of virtue may appear. David the prophet says in the Psalm: "O Lord, by Your beauty You gave strength to my beauty" (Ps 29:8). Let us be purified so that the image of God may appear in us, and this is what God wants from us, that we be without spot, without lack and without blemish.

1.10.14.en: St. Dorotheus Zaanan: some see that the prophet is playing on the word to give a symbolic meaning.

1.10.15.en: The inhabitant of Zaanan does not go out of her house, but lurks in terror awaiting her bitter fate, when the invader attacks her and takes her captive.

1.10.16.en: The city of Beth-ezel: a Hebrew name meaning "the nearby place" or "the house of separation." It is said to be "Asil," or Deir el-Asal, southwest of Hebron and about two miles east of Tell Beit Mirsim. It was most likely fortified and would resist the invader, but its people weep for what has befallen their brothers in the other cities, and grow weary from much lamenting.

1.11.0.en: For the inhabitant of Maroth waited carefully for good: but evil came down from the LORD unto the gate of Jerusalem. [12]

1.11.1.en: Maroth: it lies in western Judah, and was perhaps the same as "Maarath." Some see that this name is a play on the word "Maarath" (Josh 15:59) to give the meaning of bitterness, and that it is now called Beit Ummar.

1.11.2.en: * The things of grace are accompanied by joy, peace, love and truth... But the forms of sin are accompanied by disturbance, and neither love nor joy toward God.

1.11.3.en: St. Macarius the Great * What if a man is rich, and of the nobility? When some sin takes him captive, he becomes more corrupt than any corruption. If a man who is a king has been taken captive by barbarians, he becomes the most wretched of men; so it is with sin, for it is barbarian, and the soul that becomes a captive does not know how to free itself from captivity, and sin plays the role of a tyrant to destroy everyone who clings to it.

1.11.4.en: St. John Chrysostom O thou inhabitant of Lachish, bind the chariot to the swift beast.

1.12.0.en: She is the beginning of the sin to the daughter of Zion: for the transgressions of Israel were found in thee. [13]

1.12.1.en: Lachish: a fortified city lying in the plains of Judah (Josh 15:33, 39). It was known as Tell el-Hesi, which is about 16 miles northeast of Gaza and eleven miles northeast of Gaza and 11 southwest of Beit Jibrin.

1.12.2.en: The inhabitant of Lachish is told to flee from the coming invasion, because she was the first to drive Zion to commit sin.

1.12.3.en: Therefore shalt thou give presents to Moresheth-gath.

1.13.0.en: The houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel. [14]

1.13.1.en: "Beth Achzib" (Achzib) means "the house of deception," for it deceived the kings of Israel. It was also called Chezib (Gen 38:5), and Cozeba (1 Chr 4:22). Perhaps the city took this name from a spring in it which flowed in winter and dried up in summer. Some think that it is "Ain Kezbeh" in the Wadi el-Ilah (Valley of Elah) north of Adullam. Others say it is "Tell el-Beida" (Tell el-Beida) southwest of Adullam.

1.13.2.en: Instead of this city acting against the invaders, it will be helpless and powerless, and perhaps it will turn into a treacherous deceiver on behalf of the invader.

1.13.3.en: Yet will I bring an heir unto thee, O inhabitant of Mareshah.

1.14.0.en: He shall come unto Adullam the glory of Israel. [15]

1.14.1.en: Adullam: a Hebrew name meaning a refuge, mentioned between the towns of Jarmuth and Socoh; it is Canaanite in origin. The Canaanites dwelt in it from the days of Jacob (Gen 38:1-2). Joshua struck it, then Rehoboam fortified it (2 Chr 11:7). The Jews settled in it after the return from the captivity (Neh 11:30). Its site is Tell Sheikh Madhkur. Adullam was surrounded by rugged terrain and was famous for its caves in which men used to hide from the face of war. In it was the cave in which David hid and which he made his headquarters (1 Sam 22:1; 2 Sam 23:13; 1 Chr 11:15), and it is said that it is the cave of the Wadi Khureitun, also called the caves of Id el-Ma, about thirteen miles southwest of Bethlehem, between Lachish and Jerusalem.

1.14.2.en: Mareshah loses her honor, and the glory stops at Adullam. The prophet Micah warns them of the attack of the enemies, so that the nobles and great men of Judah are forced to flee to these caves to hide, as though the glory of Israel had been buried in these caves.

1.14.3.en: Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children.

1.15.0.en: Enlarge thy baldness as the eagle; for they are gone into captivity from thee. [16]

1.15.1.en: The prophet portrays the terrible sorrow that comes upon fathers and mothers as they see their sons and daughters taken into captivity. This happened many times, to Israel and to Judah alike, and reached its most terrible form in the final invasion of Israel by Assyria in 722 A.D., which the prophet Micah lived to see, and the final invasion of Judah in 586 B.C.

1.15.2.en: Israel is like a mother weeping for her cities as for daughters who have died and lost life, and so she declares her grief over them and over her sons who were born in honor and now are led into captivity.

1.15.3.en: Here Micah speaks of what will come to pass as one who sees it happening while he prophesies concerning them.

1.15.4.en: * This happened, as we know, since we were told beforehand concerning Judah by the prophet: "enlarge thy baldness as the eagle" (Mic 1:16); for baldness comes upon a man in his head only, but in the case of the eagle it comes upon its whole body. For when it grows very old it sheds the pinion feathers of its wings from its whole body. He (Judah) loses his feathers when he loses his people. He sheds the pinions of his wings with which he was accustomed to fly toward the prey, since all the strong men perish by whom he (Judah) swoops down upon others.

1.15.6.en: The bitterness of sin in my mouth!

1.15.7.en: * I confess to You, O my God:

1.15.8.en: I drink sin like water, and think there is life and happiness in pleasure!

1.15.9.en: Reveal to me the bitterness of sin.

1.15.10.en: Your fiery Spirit exposes my depths, so that I cling to You, O Forgiver of sin!

1.15.11.en: * You desire to judge me, not to take vengeance on me, but to chasten me in Your mercy, and to qualify me for Your eternal inheritance!

1.15.12.en: Your fatherhood, even in its firmness, is full of tenderness!

1.15.13.en: Your care is surpassing; You carry me on Your shoulders!

1.15.14.en: * Come out to me, and shatter every lofty mountain in my depths, and let all despair in my heart dissolve, and let my sin be dispersed like waters down a steep place!

1.15.15.en: Shatter my evils, and remove all corruption within me!

1.15.16.en: * As You come out to me in love, grant me to go out to my brothers!

1.15.17.en: Let me wail for a wandering soul, and howl for every lost person; how can my heart not burn for every one who stumbles?

1.15.18.en: How can I not be weak with every weak one?

1.15.19.en: How can I not count myself a captive with everyone who is captive to sin?

1.15.20.en: * I return, and my soul groans over my sins and the sins of my brothers!

1.15.21.en: I confess to You that we have caused many to stumble; let Your grace work in us, that we may glorify You for Your divine work in us!

1.15.22.en: * Our sin turned us to dust; Your grace lifts us to heaven!

1.15.23.en: * Our sin made us lose the garment of Your righteousness; Your fiery Spirit restores to us Your righteousness within us!

1.15.24.en: * Our sin robbed us of our inner peace; Your presence in us grants us Your surpassing peace!

1.15.25.en: * Our sin embittered our souls; our fellowship with You is sweetness itself!

1.15.26.en: * Our sin shattered our spiritual walls; Your indwelling is the fiery wall of our souls!

1.15.27.en: * Our sin deceived us with lies and vain promises.

1.15.28.en: Your coming down to us lifted us to Your eternal glories!

1.15.29.en: * Our sin led us into captivity; Your grace grants us the freedom of the glory of the children of God!
